entries.topicDescription: Explicit error handling patterns and best practices.

tips.title: Errors are values — check them explicitly
tips.content:
Go doesn't have exceptions. Functions that can fail return
an error as the last return value. Callers must check it
explicitly with 'if err != nil'.

This makes the error path visible and forces you to handle
it. No hidden exceptions, no unchecked throws. Every error
is dealt with where it occurs.

The error interface has a single method: Error() string.
Any type implementing this interface can be used as an error.

While the if-err-nil pattern may seem verbose, it results in
code where the happy path and error path are both explicit
and easy to follow.

tips.title: Wrap errors with fmt.Errorf and %w for context
tips.content:
When you receive an error from a lower-level function, wrap
it with additional context using fmt.Errorf and the %w verb.
This creates an error chain that preserves the original cause.

Callers can inspect the chain with errors.Is() to check for
specific error values, or errors.As() to extract a specific
error type. Both traverse the entire wrap chain.

Good error messages read like a stack trace: "opening database:
reading config: open app.json: no such file". Each layer adds
context about what operation was attempted.

Define sentinel errors (var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...)) for
expected conditions that callers should handle differently.

tips.title: Custom error types carry structured information
tips.content:
Sometimes you need more than a string message. Define a
custom error type (a struct implementing the error interface)
to carry structured data like error codes, HTTP status codes,
or field validation details.

Custom errors let callers extract specific information with
errors.As(). This is more robust than string matching and
enables programmatic error handling.

Combine custom errors with error wrapping: wrap a custom
error with fmt.Errorf to add context while preserving the
structured data for callers who need it.

This pattern is ideal for APIs where different errors need
different HTTP status codes, or validation where you need
to report which fields failed and why.
